newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil bank rescues cost proportionally less.
newsitem.headline: Brazil bank rescues cost proportionally less.

text.p: Brazil's restructuring of its banking sector has cost proportionally far less than in other Latin American and even leading developed nations that have had to salvage floundering banks, the Finance Ministry said Wednesday.

In a report on the adjustments banks have gone through in post-hyperinflation Brazil, the ministry's economics department said 20.8 billion reais had so far been handed out under the PROER program to encourage mergers in the financial sector.
In addition, 8.0 billion reais was used to rescue Latin America's largest bank, state-run Banco do Brasil.
The total Brazil has paid is therefore $28.8 billion reais, equivalent to 3.8 percent of gross domestic product.

"It's worth noting that the...money used in the process of adjustment of private banks and Banco do Brasil was, up till now, lower than those involved in the programs of adjustment of the financial sector in other countries," the report said.
The Finance Ministry did not give total dollar figures on bailout costs in other countries.
The Finance Ministry said Argentina's banking crisis had cost it 13.0 percent of GDP, Chile's 19.6 percent of GDP, Venezuela's 13.0 percent and Colombia's 6.0 percent.
In Europe, Finland paid out the equivalent of 8.2 percent of its GDP to shore up the banking system and Norway and Sweden both coughed up 4.5 percent of GDP.
The United States, according to the Brazilian Finance Ministry's report, paid the equivalent of 5.1 percent of its GDP to get through the savings and loans crisis in 1991.
PROER was set up in November 1995 and provides special low-cost credit lines to aid bank buyouts and mergers.
In summing up the program, the Finance Ministry noted the Central Bank had intervened in 40 institutions since the "Plano Real" economic stablization plan came into being.
It added that of the 271 institutions operating in Brazil at the start of the Plano Real, 72 had undergone a transfer of control, most without Central Bank intervention.
"This indicates that the adjustment of the financial system to a new macroeconomic environment has been relatively rapid," the report said.
It also stressed the 28.8 billion reais paid out did not represent the "fiscal cost" of shoring up the financial system.

"In truth, it is impossible to calculate today whether PROER will or will not have a fiscal cost," the ministry said. "This is due to the impossibility of calculating the gains and losses involved until the banking assets and guarantees in the hands of the Central Bank are cashed in over time."

The report pointed out that banks benefiting from PROER money gave guarantees worth 120 percent of the funds received and that some of those assets, such as Brady bonds, have gained in value recently.
In its conclusion, the ministry said Brazil's banking sector readjustment process seemed to consist of three stages.
The first, largely over now, was the financial rescue by the state of the private sector and transfers of control.

The second, which has already begun, is the entry into Brazil of large international institutions and the readjustment of state-owned banks. The ministry noted this stage would also see global banking groups buying into privatized state banks.
The third stage, according to the ministry, will be reforms in the way banks conduct business in Brazil.
((-- Brasilia newsroom 55-61-2230358))
